title: Mary E. Lovely on what's really going on with global supply chains
content_preview: How have US tariffs affected global supply chains? Are trading patterns between countries really changing? What can we learn from the fine print of trade agreements? Are the US and China really decoupling? PIIE Anthony M. Solomon Senior Fellow Mary E. Lovely dives into these questions and more with host Anjali V. Bhatt in this episode, exploring Lovely's recent research on global supply chains and US "reciprocal" trade agreements. They discuss lessons from past rounds of US tariffs, how global supply chains are reorganizing (or not), and more. HOST Anjali V. BhattCommunications Manager and…

title: Hormuz Shipping Remains Subdued Despite Apparent Reopening
content_preview: Politics, Geopolitics & Conflict Hormuz is “open”, but nowhere close to functioning normally. The U.S. has cleared mines from the internationally recognized shipping lanes and can technically get vessels through, but Iran’s military capability will still keep most commercial operators away. Only five commodity vessels crossed on Tuesday, compared to some 130 ships a day before the war. Iran is offering a temporary and limited corridor while making full normalization conditional on sanctions relief, an end to the U.S. blockade…

title: Oil Selloff Outruns Reality in Hormuz
content_preview: WTI crude oil futures were trading at $83.51 late Thursday, down $3.13, or 3.61%, for the week. The market opened near the weekly high at $86.57, then broke to $79.62 as traders sold on reports that Iran, Oman and the United States were moving toward a workable shipping arrangement through the Strait of Hormuz. Thursday changed the tone. WTI bounced after Iran fired on a vessel near Oman and President Trump rejected terms tied to reviving the June Iran ceasefire agreement. The market stopped trading a Hormuz reopening and started trading the fact…

title: Many school supplies cost more under Trump's tariffs
content_preview: Autumn means back-to-school shopping for many households. This year, consumers face higher prices for many basic supplies because of President Donald Trump's tariffs. Backpacks, calculators, notebooks, and shoes are among the products in six categories hit with higher tariffs since he returned to the presidency in early 2025. Nationally, the annual tariff costs for these goods are projected to average $79 higher per US household this year than in 2024.
